item.title: How could Japan shake up the global markets?
item.description:
How could Japan shake up the global markets?

Minutes from the Bank of Japan’s October meeting point to another rate hike in December, and it’s easy to see why.

The weak yen and rising energy costs driven by Middle East tensions have pushed core inflation to 2.1% year over year in September, its highest level since early 2026 and above the BOJ’s 2% target, while the measure excluding food and energy climbed to 2.4%. Higher oil pricesadd to these inflationary pressures, particularly because Japan relies heavily on energy imports. This also makes oil prices an important factor to watch when assessing the BOJ’s next policy move.

As for why the BOJ is holding back, even though the conditions for a hike are already in place, a tighter policy could help bring inflation under control and ease pressure on the yen, but it would also make borrowing more expensive, potentially cooling business activity and investment.

Another reason is Japan’s massive government debt, which exceeds 200% of GDP. Rather than paying it off, the government keeps rolling over maturing bonds by issuing new ones, while continuing to pay interest on its debt.

This means that higher rates would make that debt increasingly expensive to service, putting even more pressure on public finances and raising concerns about long-term debt sustainability. 

Currency intervention could also help ease some of this pressure. By selling US dollars and buying yen, Japan’s authorities can support the currency and curb imported inflation. Such intervention could also trigger a sharp move lower in USD/JPY, depending on its scale and how markets interpret the authorities’ intentions. The yen they receive can then be withdrawn from circulation, reducing liquidity in the economy.

The catch is that Japan’s reserves, while substantial, are not unlimited. And a large part of them is held in US Treasuries.

If Japan starts selling those bonds to support the yen rather than hiking rates, Treasury yields could climb, putting pressure on global markets, particularly riskier assets. After all, why take risks in stocks when you can earn a relatively safe 5% on government bonds?

A Fed rate cut could offer relief to both US and Japanese markets by making the yen carry trade less attractive, but with inflation still running hot and the labor market holding up, that looks unlikely for now. 

On the other hand, if the Fed does move in the opposite directionto BOJ and the carry trade unwinds, it could create another problem: investors who borrowed yen to buy foreign assets may be forced to sell them to repay their loans. This could trigger a repeat of the 2024 sell-off across markets. 

 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Why falling oil prices might not deliver the inflation relief everyone expects
item.description:
Oil prices are starting to fall again, so surely that must mean our cost-of-living problems should be disappearing too, right? Well, if only the economics behind that were so straightforward and cooperative.

WTI crude has dropped back to just below $86 today amid hopes of easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. That is welcome news for households especially after the energy shock this year and I can understand why markets are getting excited as well.

But before popping the champagne, this is something worth remembering. Cheaper oil doesn't necessarily mean cheaper living.

Sure, lower oil prices should eventually bring some relief to let's say the gasoline pump. That means transportation and shipping costs could also ease, affording businesses a little bit more breathing room.

But here's something to think about. When was the last time that your rent, insurance bill or favourite restaurant actually became cheaper? Dum, dum, dum. Exactly. And this is precisely where the inflation story gets a little more complicated beyond just falling oil prices.

Just take a look at the chart above. Since January 2020, gasoline prices have jumped by nearly 68% while food and shelter costs have risen by around 35% and 34% respectively in the US. Meanwhile, overall consumer prices have increased by roughly 31%.

Now, here's the interesting bit. Nominal wages have also risen by nearly 34% during the same period, slightly outpacing overall inflation. On paper, that suggests the average worker should be a little better off, no? Well, not quite.

The fact of the matter is that we don't all spend our money the same way. If you're spending a bigger chunk of your income on things like groceries, rent and gasoline, then those price increases can still sting. And a cheaper tank of gasoline today isn't going to magically reverse years of higher living costs.

Anyway, let's put aside the numbers and focus on what's really important here. At the end of the day, inflation coming down doesn't mean prices are coming down. It simply means that prices are still rising, just more slowly.

So even if gasoline prices are to fall today, that doesn't undo years of increases in housing, food, healthcare and other essential expenses. And then there's another twist to all of this too. Cheaper fuel leaves consumers with more money to spend elsewhere, potentially supporting demand and keeping some price pressures alive.

So, what does all this mean for the Fed?

I think it's relatively straightforward. Falling oil prices can help to ease the pressure showing up on headline inflation. However, policymakers need to see broader improvements in underlying price pressures before they can feel comfortable changing course.

With that in mind, I would argue that markets ought to pay more attention to things like core services inflation, wage growth, and Treasury yields as compared to watching out for the next $5 or $10 drop in oil prices.

If the next inflation reports show genuine signs of cooling beyond energy, only then markets might have reason to rethink the Fed's policy outlook. But if services inflation stays stubborn, then cheaper oil on its own probably won't be able to move the needle much.

That's sort of the irony of it all now, isn't it? Oil prices might be falling again but the inflation problem isn't necessarily going to follow in that same direction.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: India October CPI inflation rises to 6.09%, food inflation accelerates to 8.94%
item.description:
• India CPI Y/Y 6.09% vs 5.93% expected
  • Prior 5.54%
  • Full report

India's CPI rose to 6.09% y/y in October, according to provisional data, pointing to increased price pressures in the economy. The headline inflation rate was higher in rural areas, where prices increased by 6.63% y/y, compared with 5.41% in urban areas.

Food inflation was a big standout, with the Consumer Food Price Index rising 8.94% y/y in October. Food price increases were relatively broad-based across the country, with rural food inflation reaching 9.09% and urban food inflation standing at 8.68%.

The figures highlight the significant contribution of food prices to India's inflationary pressures, with food inflation running well above the headline CPI rate. Overall, the October report points to a challenging inflation environment for the Reserve Bank of India. Given the acceleration in inflation, the market is pricing in a 69% chance of a 25 bps hike at the next RBI meeting, with 31% probabilitiy of a larger 50 bps move. 

The US-Iran war has been a major contributor of inflation through higher crude oil prices, increasing India's import bill and raising transportation, energy and agricultural production costs.

As a major oil importer, India is particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the Middle East. Higher energy and fertiliser costs gradually feed into consumer prices, while a weaker rupee also makes imports more expensive.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil is caught between hopes of de-escalation and concerns of further escalation. What's next?
item.description:
Crude oil has been consolidating around recent lows as the US-Iran uncertainty keeps traders guessing on the next move.

The US-Iran conflict remains the main driver of course, with diplomatic efforts showing some signs of progress but no concrete breakthrough yet.

Oil prices dipped yesterday after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US Vice President Vance was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official in an effort to end the war.

However, significant mistrust remains, with Iranian officials accusing Washington of preparing further military strikes or tighter economic pressure. Iran has also continued to issue warnings of retaliation against US military bases and reportedly targeted ship navigation systems near the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, the US military says its blockade has prevented Iran from exporting oil, while US forces are working to keep the Strait open to commercial shipping. The conflicting signals leave the outlook highly uncertain, with oil prices remaining sensitive to any developments that could either pave the way for de-escalation or trigger another escalation.

It goes without saying that a concrete breakthrough would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly. But an escalation, on the other hand, could trigger another rally on a rising risk premium, although there’s also a chance that it could be short-lived if Trump launches limited strikes just to save face before exiting the war.

item.title: Chart of the day: USD/JPY nears 160.00 as technical warning signs raise Japan intervention risks
item.description:
Well, it looks like dollar bulls are starting to play with fire again. USD/JPY is creeping back towards the 160.00 level and while the move might look like another show of strength for the dollar, I suspect that Japanese authorities aren't finding it quite as amusing.

And from a technical perspective, there are reasons why Tokyo officials might be getting a tad bit nervous this week.

After spending much of October repeatedly struggling to really test the 159.00 level and with repeated failed attempts in getting above the 200-day moving average (blue line), USD/JPY has finally pushed past those key resistance levels. Buyers had been knocking on the same door for weeks but are now finally managing a breakthrough.

And with price pushing past both the key daily moving averages in the latest run higher, the technical picture is threatening to open up towards 160.00 next.

However, this is where things start to get a little more dicey for USD/JPY and dollar bulls. The 160.00 mark isn't just another technical level. These sort of big psychological barriers and figure levels are often a potential trigger point for Japanese authorities to step up their intervention warnings or even potentially act outright.

This was precisely where we saw intervention action back during late April and early May. And with USD/JPY now approaching that territory again, the technical break above 159.00 provides a rather clear reason for Tokyo officials to worry about the yen's renewed depreciation.

At least for now, the fundamental backdrop isn't helping with the latest predicament either. Hotter US inflation and a more hawkish Fed outlook continue to favour the dollar, even as markets are pricing in roughly 73% odds of another BOJ rate hike in December. The fact of the matter is that markets were expecting the BOJ to be more bold in stepping up their pace of tightening, but policymakers have appeared to be reluctant to pre-commit or push too aggressively on the matter.

Now of course, intervention isn't automatically triggered by a particular USD/JPY level. Tokyo officials have repeatedly emphasised that the speed and nature of currency moves are more important than any specific level. In other words, they just don't want things to go too far, too fast.

That being said, I wouldn't dismiss the warning signs here. And I would be surprised if we do see USD/JPY run up above 160.00 at the first time of asking, unless we do get some added surprise in terms of headlines or another broader bid in the dollar across the major currencies space.

For now, traders will do well to trade with caution and assess the danger near the 160.00 mark until there is a good enough reason to dip their toes in the water above the figure level.

At this juncture, it would be reasonable to expect USD/JPY to trade more cautiously just below 160.00 with some potential for profit-taking and some sudden 20-30 pips moves. That especially since any notable push higher in USD/JPY near or above the 160.00 level is arguably enough of a reason for Tokyo to come in and spoil the party. So, just be mindful of that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

As a reminder, the drop was triggered by the surprisingly hawkish remarks from Fed’s Waller where not only he said that he would vote for a rate hike in December regardless of the inflation data but he also put on the table a 50 bps hike in case the data came in higher than expected.

The losses then extended after the US CPI came indeed hotter than expected and raised the probabilities for a 50 bps hike. Fed’s Hammack spoke after the CPI data and she also left a door open for a larger rate hike. At the moment, traders are pricing in just a 12% chance of a 50 bps hike but the probabilities could rise further in case more Fed members support such a move or don’t push back against this possibility.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. The WSJ reported that US Vice President Vance is considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official in an effort to end the war.

In separate reports, Iranian senior officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic pressure to push Iran into retaliatory actions. Overall, there’s understandably lots of mistrust, but it reinforces the view that a deal is not as near as the market expected.

Looking ahead, I would expect rate hikes to put even more downward pressure on the stock market and long-term Treasury yields amid increased growth concerns, barring an end to the Iran war. This could ultimately be positive for gold.

Keep in mind that in the current context, if Trump decides to escalate the war, inflation expectations would rise alongside weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. item.title: European stock market open: DAX pushes to fresh record highs as Europe defies Wall Street jitters
item.description:
Europe's stock market party is showing no signs of winding down with the DAX is leading the celebrations on the week. Germany's benchmark index is up another 1.0% at the open, pushing to fresh record highs even as Wall Street looks set for yet another troubling session.

Here's how European indices are faring at the open:

  • Eurostoxx +0.3%
  • Germany DAX +1.0%
  • France CAC 40 +0.6%
  • UK FTSE +0.3%
  • Spain IBEX flat
  • Italy FTSE MIB -0.2%

It's not exactly a clean sweep but European investors certainly have more reasons to smile than their US counterparts this morning at least. S&P 500 futures are down 0.4% while Nasdaq futures are falling 0.9% as tech stocks are once again looking vulnerable following the recent attempts to recover from last week's brutal selloff.

Nvidia was the poster boy of the AI rally but amid CEO Jensen Huang's affair scandals (yes, with an 's' now), the chipmaker is facing heavy scrutiny with shares down another 6.5% in pre-market. If that is sustained, the open will see Nvidia fall to its lowest since July 2025. Ouch.

Anyway, the fact that the DAX is cruising along and pushing to fresh record highs suggests that investors aren't simply treating Europe as a passenger in Wall Street's rally anymore. That being said, there's still a fair bit of unevenness beneath the surface with Spain and Italy slipping slightly. However, both indices have also recovered well to erase the entirety of their respective declines in October. So, there's that.

Falling oil prices and geopolitical relief have helped to give European stocks a good nuge earlier in the week and that mood has persisted since, alongside more resilient corporate earnings in Q3. Investors have took to that and are still not letting go as we get into the second half of the week.

Perhaps there is also a sneaky bit of rotation play with US tech stocks having encountered much volatility in the past weeks and suddenly investors are rushing across the Atlantic? There is that to consider as well, although European equities have their own set of challenges amid growing fiscal risks in France, higher borrowing costs, and also a potential stagflation problem that may be building.

Circling back to the market open today, Europe is still very much dancing to its own tune. The DAX is setting the pace but the real test will be whether the rest of the region can keep up if Wall Street's tech troubles continue to deepen.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold price faces a key test as $4,000 breaks and weekly support beckons
item.description:
It's not been a good week for gold. Just as it seemed like buyers might be looking to take a peek at a firmer run above $4,000, they are now being dragged back to the danger zone. After all the pushing and pulling this week, gold is now finding itself staring down a rather uncomfortable test just below the figure level.

The drop since overnight trading sees the precious metal move to $3,960 now, as the dollar continues to flex its muscles. The stronger-than-expected US CPI report earlier this week has certainly complicated matters, with traders now having to contend with a more hawkish Fed outlook alongside higher Treasury yields. Yes, the bond market is back in action today and 10-year yields are still keeping at 5%.

Overall, that's hardly the sort of combination gold buyers would be hoping for - especially with the technical picture also starting to look rather fragile.

Looking at the weekly chart, gold is now approaching a crucial support region around $3,900 to $3,930. That includes the 100-week moving average (red line), which is currently sitting at $3,897, alongside the recent swing lows from July and September. The confluence of these technical levels makes this region a rather important line in the sand for buyers.

A firm break below the support region could open the door for a deeper correction towards $3,500 next, with the broader bullish trend then facing a much sterner test. For some context, the last time that gold decisively broke below any of its key weekly moving averages was all the way back in October 2023. So, that speaks to just how much momentum buyers had been riding on over the past two years especially.

On the flip side, holding above the 100-week moving average would at least offer buyers some breathing room to regroup. But even so, I would argue that reclaiming $4,000 alone won't be enough to turn the mood around. The recent lower highs suggest that sellers are still maintaining control for the most part, with the $4,200 level standing in the way of a more meaningful recovery. Beyond that, $4,600 remains the next major resistance hurdle for gold buyers.

For now, the big question is whether buyers can defend the key support region that has been keeping the broader bullish structure intact. And they certainly have their work cut out with the dollar and Fed rate expectations working against them as we approach the latter stages this week. It's squeaky bum time.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Production accounted for another 0.01% contribution, with construction being a drag with a negative contribution of -0.04%. At the balance, that sees the UK economy grow by 0.7% (rounded) in the three months to September.

The September monthly report shows that the economy is holding up in wrapping up the third quarter, despite fears of more uneven growth conditions before that.

As such, that will allow the BOE to keep majority their focus on the inflation battle as economic conditions point to some resilience at least for now. With markets pricing in roughly 71% odds of another rate hike in December, the GDP figures today will do little to dissuade that and keep traders locked in for another potential move by the central bank before year-end.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq futures are under pressure. Is it too late to short?
item.description:
With futures near 28,185, the first downside target is just 20 points away. A rebound toward 28,232–28,284 would give sellers a different risk-reward setup.

Nasdaq-100 futures | November 12, 2026 | Overnight session

With Nasdaq-100 futures near 28,185 at my overnight snapshot, I’d wait for a bounce before considering a short. The first target is already close, while the level that would invalidate the idea is 152 points higher. I’m watching three prices where a rebound could give sellers a better entry.

Nvidia was down 7.7% and AMD was up 1.75% in that snapshot. Bitcoin was also softer near $73,600. The weakness in Bitcoin adds to the risk-off tone, while AMD’s gain shows that some chip stocks are holding up through the Nvidia selloff. I covered the initial move in my earlier report on Nvidia’s after-hours decline.

Three levels for a possible Nasdaq short

These are sell-limit levels. They depend on a rebound and may fill individually or in combination. If futures slide straight to the first target before any entry fills, I’d pass on the setup.

  • 28,232 | First entry. A 47-point bounce from the snapshot would bring the first order into play.
  • 28,254 | Second entry. Just above the developing session VWAP, the average traded price weighted by volume.
  • 28,284 | Third entry. Closer to the first band above VWAP and still below the developing value area high, near 28,300.
  • 28,337 | Stop. Above both the developing value area high and the second upper VWAP band at the snapshot. If buyers reclaim 28,300 and hold above it, the case for selling the bounce weakens. 28,337 is the planned exit if the short is open.

The session’s VWAP and both value-area boundaries move as trading continues. If the rebound comes later and those references have shifted materially, I’d reassess the setup before using the same orders.

Where I’d look to take profits

  • 28,165 | First target. Just above the prior session’s value area low. If a short is open and price reaches this level, I’d consider taking partial profits, cancelling any unfilled sell orders and moving the stop on the remainder to the average price of the entries that actually filled.
  • 27,957 | Second target. Above an earlier session’s point of control, the price where the most volume traded.
  • 27,837 | Third target. Just ahead of the November 10 point of control and VWAP. That’s the last target in the main plan.

What waiting changes about the trade

At 28,185, a short would have 20 points to the first target against 152 points to the stop, or about 0.13R. If only the first limit at 28,232 fills, that improves to 0.64R. If all three entries fill in equal size, the average entry is approximately 28,256.67, with 80.33 points of initial risk. The three targets are then about 1.14R, 3.73R and 5.22R, respectively, before fees and slippage. Each figure measures the distance to that target against the initial risk. The overall result depends on how much of the position comes off at each level.

I’d keep the size small. CME’s Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (MNQ) are worth $2 per point. One micro at each entry would put $482 at risk if all three filled and the stop executed at 28,337, before fees and slippage. A stop moved to the average entry can still slip. If you trade a Nasdaq CFD, check its quote and value per point before using this futures map.

The trade-off I’m willing to live with is missing a trade while I wait for a better entry. Chasing a short after a sharp drop can put you underwater on the first bounce. A patient entry can improve the reward relative to the risk, and you can still get filled and stopped out. Some days, the market moves without you, and that’s part of the plan.

For more on managing pending orders and partial exits, see the investingLive guide to using tradeCompass.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ policymaker Asada urges caution on further rate hikes even as December move remains firmly in play
item.description:
BOJ board member, Toichiro Asada, still isn't quite ready to jump on the rate hike bandwagon it would seem. The central bank's resident dove is once again preaching caution, warning that further tightening could undermine the progress that Japan has made in achieving sustainable inflation.

Here are his latest remarks from today:

  • Inflation has already reached roughly 2%, leaving little reason to push prices higher
  • BOJ must be cautious about raising interest rates too quickly
  • Further rate hikes may be necessary in the future, but should be carried out slowly
  • Not opposed to raising rates altogether and is not considering proposing a rate cut
  • Japan's neutral interest rate may be somewhat above the current policy rate
  • Has no specific terminal interest rate in mind
  • Policy decisions should be assessed at every meeting, considering economic risks and financial conditions
  • BOJ could still raise or lower rates even after reaching a level consistent with its inflation target
  • BOJ does not directly control exchange rates (declines to specify a desirable USD/JPY level)
  • Further tightening risks weakening underlying inflation, particularly as consumption continues to lack momentum

Now, I wouldn't read too much into the dovish undertones here. After all, Asada's call for caution is somewhat consistent with the BOJ's broader policy communication in saying that future rate decisions will be guided by incoming economic data and financial conditions.

Besides, Asada is also known to have a more dovish view after having opposed the June and September rate hikes. As such, his reservations here aren't exactly all too surprising.

As things stand, markets are still pricing in roughly 73% odds of another 25 bps rate hike in December. So, that tells us traders are still somewhat convinced that there is further tightening to follow before the year is over and done with.

That being said, a lot can change in four weeks and we'll have to see how the rest of the BOJ board set out their convictions in the weeks ahead.

For the Japanese yen, the immediate implications from Asada's comments are limited. With USD/JPY hovering near 160.00, the bigger influences remain the widening contrast between the Fed and BOJ outlooks as well as intervention risks.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUD/USD faces a make-or-break test as dollar bulls turn up the heat
item.description:
With the dollar finding its swagger again this week, AUD/USD is now staring down a rather uncomfortable date with its March lows. The question now is will buyers finally put their foot down or are we about to see another major leg lower in the currency pair?

We're seeing price drop to around 0.6835 currently, putting the March lows at 0.6833 firmly in the spotlight. A firm break below that will see AUD/USD fall to its lowest levels since January, potentially opening the door for a push towards 0.6800 and below next.

After failing to sustain a recovery above 0.7000 at the end of last month, sellers have firmly regained control in AUD/USD. The pair has since broken back below its key daily moving averages and the rising trendline support from the March to June lows that had helped underpin the upside momentum since July.

That leaves the March low at 0.6833 as the next major line in the sand. Below that, the 0.6800 level comes into focus with little obvious technical support until the January trading region. The 100-week moving average at 0.6700 might offer buyers a place to lean on amid such a break lower next.

And looking at the fundamental backdrop, there isn't much encouragement for the aussie either.

The dollar resurgence continues to gather momentum after hotter US inflation and more hawkish Fed remarks reinforced expectations for another rate hike in December. Meanwhile, the RBA looks to have moved to the sidelines after its latest move and that leaves the Fed being the one with the more immediate tightening bias.

And when you throw in a deteriorating risk mood with US futures turning sour again, it's hardly the friendliest environment for the risk-sensitive aussie currency.

As such, what I'll be watching now is whether sellers can secure a daily close below 0.6833. A brief dip could still invite some bargain hunting but a sustained break would strengthen the bearish case considerably.

As for buyers, reclaiming 0.6900 would be a first step towards stabilising sentiment. But until then, sellers look firmly in the driver's seat and they could very well take the pair much lower in getting to their next destination.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chinese tech firms reportedly rushing to secure more Nvidia chip capacity amid fears that spy scandal would spur tighter restrictions
item.description:
Well, talk about a scandal sending everyone scrambling for the exits. Except in this case, Chinese tech firms aren't exactly looking to leave the party. Instead, they're trying to grab as much Nvidia computing power as they can before Washington potentially slams the door shut.

Reuters is reporting that AI companies in China are looking to secure more Nvidia-powered cloud computing capacity at overseas data centres, fearing that the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang could accelerate tougher US restrictions, citing three people familiar with the matter.

The sources noted that a major Chinese cloud provider has reportedly discussed locking in overseas capacity, while smaller AI firms are exploring similar arrangements - particularly in Southeast Asia.

And there's good reason that Chinese tech firms are getting nervous here. For some context, the US already restricts China's access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips. However, these companies have been able to work around some of those restrictions by renting computing power from data centres outside the country.

The fear now is that at some point, that very loophole could soon become a casualty of the latest political fallout.

Essentially, Huang's latest affair scandal and controversy with a woman who is suspected to be a Chinese spy has given lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for tighter export controls.

One particular concern is the proposed Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would give Washington greater authority to regulate overseas cloud access to restricted US technology. The legislation on this passed the House in January and is awaiting Senate action currently.

Besides that, Reuters also reports that grey-market buyers in China are stockpiling restricted Nvidia processors amid fears of a broader crackdown on chip smuggling.

When it rains, it really does pour. And it's not just Nvidia that is feeling the pressure here.

If the US does move to restrict overseas cloud access, then Chinese AI developers could face higher computing costs and tighter capacity constraints. Meanwhile, Nvidia and overseas data-centre operators are at risk of losing access to an important customer base.

That's going to be a rough one and could shake the relatively fragile AI sentiment even more to end the week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia stock plunges 8.6%, but AMD and Broadcom rally. Which chip stocks are worth buying?
item.description:
Nvidia plunges 8.6% after hours. AMD and Broadcom rise, but their valuations tell another story

I'm keeping a very close eye on the escalating tech volatility today, starting with the fact that Nasdaq futures slid 0.8% following WSJ reports that Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang.

That leadership uncertainty is already triggering rapid analyst recalibrations, with Bernstein becoming the third broker in two days to step back, slashing their Nvidia price target to $200 (!)

While the market digests the fallout at the top of the AI hardware chain, I'm watching the immediate competitive ripples, specifically how Google's TPUs could capture market share from this turmoil to build a $50 billion opportunity.

Despite the turbulence in GPU leadership, broader AI infrastructure and frontier models remain incredibly resilient; I need to see if buyers step up, especially given that CoreWeave surged impressively after its latest earnings report, and institutional demand is running hot with the Anthropic IPO already heavily oversubscribed ahead of its massive $90 billion listing.

The latest reports about Jensen Huang have put Nvidia's leadership under scrutiny just days before earnings. Semiconductor stocks are reacting very differently, creating opportunities and risks for traders. But comparing their valuations reveals a less obvious investment picture.

Nvidia's leadership crisis has divided the semiconductor sector. In Wednesday's late after-hours trading, NVDA fell 8.62%, while AMD gained 4.32% and Broadcom advanced 2.39%. That gives traders two clear relative-strength candidates, but investors face a more complicated question: Why is Nvidia trading at a substantially lower forward earnings multiple than some of its potential beneficiaries?

Nvidia's problem is no longer just about Jensen Huang's personal conduct

On November 11, The New York Times reported an alleged second extramarital relationship involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a company vice president who reports directly to him.

The allegations have not been independently established, and Nvidia has not publicly confirmed the reported relationship.

More consequential for shareholders, Reuters reported that Nvidia's board was meeting late Wednesday to consider whether to remove Huang as CEO. No completed removal had been confirmed at the time of this analysis.

This represents an important escalation from November 8, when Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation while expressing confidence in Huang's leadership. The board also stated that it had no reason to believe Nvidia's secrets or national security had been compromised.

For shareholders, the issue is now leadership continuity at one of the world's most important technology companies.

And there is another complication. The Information reports that the U.S. Commerce Department is finalizing additional restrictions intended to prevent Chinese AI companies from remotely accessing advanced chips through overseas data centers. These proposed measures introduce a separate regulatory risk, making it difficult to attribute Nvidia's entire price decline to the leadership controversy.

An extraordinary divergence in semiconductor stocks

NVDA after hours

-8.62%

$158.76

AMD after hours

+4.32%

$576.76

AVGO after hours

+2.39%

$353.47

AMD outperformed Nvidia by almost 13% (!) during the observed after-hours period. Broadcom outperformed by 11% so that is an exceptional short-term divergence among major semiconductor companies.

Nvidia's decline also implies approximately $361 billion of market capitalization lost relative to Wednesday's regular-session close, based on the Finviz closing valuation. This is a change in implied equity value, not $361 billion of cash leaving the company.

But AMD and Broadcom are not necessarily receiving that capital. Rising share prices do not prove that money is directly rotating out of Nvidia into its competitors.

What the reaction does show is a willingness to distinguish between individual semiconductor companies rather than sell everything related to artificial intelligence.

Semiconductor stock valuations: Which opportunities come at a reasonable price?

The following comparison uses Finviz valuation metrics from November 11's regular-session close alongside the later after-hours price changes.

Forward P/E compares the stock price with estimated future earnings, P/S compares market value with revenue, and EV/EBITDA compares enterprise value with operating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Multiples reflect regular-session closing valuations, not recalculated after-hours values. Forward estimates can change.

The surprising observation is Nvidia's valuation.

Despite the company's dominant position in AI computing, its Finviz forward P/E of 11 is considerably below AMD's 31.33 and Broadcom's 17.87.

Nvidia also trades at approximately 20.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA, compared with AMD's 81.1 times.

This does not automatically make Nvidia the better investment. Different earnings forecasts, product mixes, capital requirements and expected growth rates explain part of the valuation gap.

However, it challenges an easy assumption that investors should simply abandon Nvidia and buy whichever competitor is rising.

An expensive stock can continue outperforming. A cheaper stock can become cheaper still when investors are uncertain about leadership, future earnings or regulatory exposure.

AMD: The clearest potential competitive beneficiary, but not a bargain

AMD is arguably the most obvious direct competitor for investors to investigate.

Unlike Nvidia, AMD does not face the same company-specific leadership controversy. It also has a growing presence in data-center accelerators and CPUs.

There is fundamental evidence supporting the interest.

According to AMD's November 3 earnings release, third-quarter data-center revenue reached $8.5 billion, up 97% year over year, supported by its Instinct GPU and EPYC processor businesses.

That growth provides a stronger investment argument than merely hoping customers become nervous about Nvidia.

Still, AMD's valuation is demanding. Its forward P/E exceeds Nvidia's by nearly three times, and its EV/EBITDA is approximately four times as high.

For investors, AMD needs to continue delivering exceptional growth to justify that premium.

For traders, the immediate test on Thursday is whether the stock can maintain its relative strength when regular U.S. trading resumes, rather than surrender Wednesday's after-hours gains.

Broadcom: A different way to invest in the AI spending cycle

Broadcom offers a somewhat different opportunity.

Its exposure to custom AI accelerators, networking infrastructure and enterprise software means it is not simply another supplier of Nvidia-style GPUs.

That diversification may be attractive to investors concerned about Nvidia-specific execution and leadership risks.

Broadcom's September quarterly report showed AI semiconductor revenue of $16.7 billion, up 221% year over year, with management forecasting continued growth in its next fiscal quarter.

At a forward P/E of 17.87, Broadcom trades below AMD's multiple but above Nvidia's.

It is not inexpensive on every measure, especially price-to-sales. Nevertheless, Broadcom combines demonstrated AI-related revenue growth with exposure to customer-designed chips and networking.

Its positive after-hours reaction makes it a leading candidate for continued relative-strength monitoring.

Micron, Marvell and TSMC: Potential casualties or opportunities?

Micron (MU): A low multiple with a cyclical warning

Micron fell 2.76% after hours despite a Finviz forward P/E of only 3.84.

That valuation looks strikingly low, particularly alongside strong reported revenue growth.

But memory earnings are cyclical, and unusually low forward multiples can reflect expectations that profits are approaching a cyclical peak. Micron also benefits from AI demand beyond Nvidia alone.

Investors should examine the sustainability of memory prices and profitability before interpreting the multiple as evidence of undervaluation.

Marvell (MRVL): Attractive AI infrastructure exposure, but weak relative price action

Marvell declined 3.00%.

Its custom silicon and interconnect exposure could make it an alternative beneficiary of AI investment, but the after-hours reaction suggests investors were not treating it as an immediate winner.

At 23.19 times forward earnings and 52.49 times EV/EBITDA, Marvell does not offer an obvious valuation discount.

A recovery that begins outperforming the broader semiconductor sector would improve the case.

TSMC (TSM): A potentially more neutral way to own AI manufacturing

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing fell 1.95% after hours.

Because TSMC manufactures chips for multiple leading designers, including Nvidia and AMD, competition between those customers does not necessarily damage TSMC's business.

Its forward P/E of 17.89 and EV/EBITDA of 17.98 are also more moderate than AMD's.

The important risk is different: if uncertainty translates into weaker overall AI investment, manufacturing demand could eventually be affected regardless of which chip designer wins.

TSMC therefore deserves attention as a potentially more diversified semiconductor opportunity, not an automatic beneficiary of Nvidia's difficulties.

What traders should watch on Thursday, November 12

The first question is whether Wednesday's extended-hours divergence survives the regular trading session.

Nvidia: Does the breakdown hold?

NVDA closed the regular session at $173.73 before falling to $158.76 after hours.

The latter is below the $164.27 regular-session 52-week low shown in the November 11 data. That makes $164.27 a useful reference for assessing whether buyers can recover territory lost during the selloff.

A sustained recovery above that reference would weaken the immediate bearish case. Continuing to trade below it would leave Nvidia vulnerable to further volatility.

Wednesday's $173.73 close is another reference for measuring how much of the overnight decline has been reversed, not a guaranteed gap-filling target.

AMD and Broadcom: Do buyers defend the relative strength?

Watch whether their gains hold despite potential weakness in the Nasdaq and semiconductor benchmarks.

If both continue outperforming, that would support the interpretation that investors are differentiating between AI companies.

If those gains quickly reverse, it could indicate that the after-hours excitement was temporary rather than the beginning of a more durable change in relative performance.

The semiconductor supply chain: Does weakness spread?

Micron, Marvell, TSMC and other chip-related stocks offer a useful comparison.

Their behavior can help distinguish an Nvidia-specific valuation adjustment from a broader reassessment of AI spending.

This also matters for companies further along the AI infrastructure chain. As investingLive discussed in its recent CoreWeave post-earnings analysis, strong AI demand does not eliminate concerns about financing, capital expenditure or profitability.

Nvidia's November 17 earnings could become an even bigger event

Nvidia is scheduled to discuss its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at 5 p.m. ET, according to its investor relations calendar.

That creates two distinct questions for investors.

The first concerns company leadership: Will Huang remain CEO, and will the board provide a credible plan for stability?

The second is financial: Does Nvidia's revenue growth, profitability and outlook continue to justify confidence in its dominant competitive position?

The two questions are related but not identical.

A change in CEO would not automatically reduce demand for Nvidia chips. Likewise, exceptionally strong earnings would not, by themselves, resolve governance or national-security concerns.

For longer-term investors, a lower share price could become attractive if the business outlook remains intact and leadership uncertainty diminishes.

For short-term traders, however, volatile news-driven conditions require more caution than an apparently attractive valuation multiple.

The central takeaway: AMD and Broadcom are the most obvious relative-strength candidates after Wednesday's reaction. Nvidia itself may deserve renewed examination on valuation, but only with full recognition of the unresolved leadership risks. Micron and TSMC warrant further fundamental investigation rather than automatic classification as losers.

The next U.S. session should help show whether the market is selectively reassessing Nvidia or beginning to question the broader AI investment cycle.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: UK September GDP in focus but will weak growth really stop the BOE from hiking again?
item.description:
The UK September monthly and latest quarterly GDP report are due at 0700 GMT today and the question that markets will be asking is just how bad would the numbers have to be to convince the BOE to take its foot off the rate hike pedal?

The estimates are pointing to a flat reading after the economy expanded by just 0.1% in August. And that follows from the more encouraging 0.4% increase in July, suggesting that growth momentum is becoming rather uneven in the past quarter.

That being said, the bigger picture isn't quite as soft as the latest monthly numbers might suggest. The UK economy expanded by 0.7% in the three months to August, largely supported by services activity. Meanwhile, manufacturing and construction have also been keeping pace, albeit less convincingly.

Besides the monthly figures, we'll also be getting the preliminary Q3 GDP estimate. So, that should ffer a better sense of whether the economy is holding up or starting to buckle under the weight of higher borrowing costs and surging energy prices. The latter have seen some better developments in the past week but will still need time to filter through back to the economy.

At the balance, a downside surprise in the numbers could weigh on sterling and temper expectations for further BOE tightening. But unless we see a particularly ugly set of numbers, I reckon that today's report will do little to materially change up the BOE's plans for December at this juncture.

Markets are currently pricing in roughly 71% odds of another 25 bps rate hike next month, following the November move to bring the bank rate to 4.25%. The reason for such aggressive pricing remains rather straightforward, and that is inflation is still the bigger problem here.

UK headline annual inflation climbed to 3.5% in September while core annual inflation rose to 2.8%, with services inflation proving stubborn at 3.7%. And as things stand, the BOE is also projecting headline inflation to reach around 5% by the middle of next year. That's hardly a comforting backdrop as we approach the final stages this year.

As such, policymakers are being left with a rather uncomfortable balancing act. Weakening growth prospects may eventually force the central bank into a more difficult decision but for now, the bigger danger is allowing inflation pressures to become more entrenched.

In that lieu, it might require considerably more than just one disappointing growth report to change the more hawkish course that the BOE is set on at the moment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Summary:

  • Nvidia fell about 7% after hours as reports said its board is weighing whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang. Bernstein, Baird and Morgan Stanley stepped back from the stock
  • Rival chipmakers AMD and Broadcom gained after hours, and Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 0.8%, against about 0.3% for S&P 500 futures
  • Asian chip stocks held up: Samsung rose almost 2% and SK Hynix 0.8%, while the Nikkei and Topix edged higher and the Hang Seng fell almost 1%
  • Japan’s October producer prices beat forecasts at 7.1% y/y, BoJ board member Asada urged caution on the pace of hikes, and Mimura warned that FX moves are too rapid, with USD/JPY near 160
  • Deutsche Bank now sees three straight Fed hikes, UBS sees two, and CBA expects higher US yields
  • Oil eased, with OPEC output back near prewar levels, and Strategy slipped after MSCI confirmed its removal from global indexes

Nvidia

Nvidia dominated the session. Its shares were around $161 in after-hours trading, down about 7%, after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s board is preparing to oust chief executive Jensen Huang. Reuters said the board was meeting on Wednesday to decide his future, and no decision had been announced at the time of writing. The reports followed a New York Times account that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, an executive who reports to him. The board was already investigating his ties to a businesswoman whom US officials identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Wall Street analysts have moved quickly. Bernstein’s Stacy Rasgon downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform and halved his price target to $200. He left his earnings forecasts unchanged and cut the valuation multiple instead, saying AI demand remains very strong but that the leadership risk is not yet fully understood. Baird had already downgraded the stock to Neutral with a $200 target, and Morgan Stanley also stepped back.

The selling has not hit the whole AI trade evenly. Rivals AMD and Broadcom rose after hours. Bloomberg Intelligence said Google’s TPU chips could win share if customers diversify away from Nvidia, and it sees TPU sales topping $50 billion in 2027. Super Micro Computer, CoreWeave and Oracle, which depend heavily on Nvidia hardware, fell. Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 0.8%, against about 0.3% for S&P 500 futures.

The calendar next week is busy. Nvidia reports results on November 17, three House committee chairs have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18, and Anthropic’s market debut is expected on November 19, with Nvidia among its private placement buyers.

Asian equities

Asia’s chip supply chain held up better than US futures suggested it might. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics rose almost 2% and SK Hynix gained about 0.8%, helping the Kospi edge up about 0.4%, although the tech-heavy Kosdaq slipped about 0.8%. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 rose about 0.25% to around 61,400 and the Topix gained about 0.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell almost 1%, while the Shanghai Composite added about 0.2%. Overall, the moves suggest investors are treating the Nvidia shock as a governance problem specific to the company, not a verdict on AI demand.

Japan

Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 7.1% from a year earlier in October, above the 6.5% forecast. Oil, chemicals, steel and utilities drove the gain, and a weak yen lifted yen-based import prices by about 25% y/y. The data strengthen the case for a Bank of Japan hike in December.

Not everyone on the board is in a hurry. Policy board member Toichiro Asada, who voted against both of this year’s hikes, said in a speech that policy is already within the estimated neutral range and that the Bank should give due consideration to the pace of further increases.

Currency officials stepped up their warnings. Atsushi Mimura, vice finance minister for international affairs, said currency moves over recent days had been too rapid. USD/JPY traded in a narrow range just below 160, around 159.70, a level that preceded actual intervention twice this year.

US rates and the Fed

Banks continued to adjust to Tuesday’s hot US inflation report. Deutsche Bank expects quarter-point Fed hikes in December, January and March. UBS keeps a base case of hikes in December and March and sees limited support for a 50 basis point move, despite Governor Christopher Waller raising the idea. Commonwealth Bank of Australia said Treasury yields have room to rise, as growth and Fed hike expectations outweigh the drag from lower oil prices.

Oil and gold

Oil eased, with Brent down about 1.4% to around $91.40 and WTI down about 1.3% to around $85.40. OPEC data showed the group’s crude output rising by nearly 2 million barrels a day in October, close to prewar levels, as Saudi Arabia lifted production to around 10.6 million barrels a day using pipelines and other workarounds. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain far below normal. Spot gold slipped about 0.3% to around $3,987 an ounce, holding below $4,000 as Fed hike expectations weigh on the metal.

Strategy

Strategy shares were around $119 after hours, down about 2.6%, after MSCI confirmed it will remove the bitcoin treasury company from its global indexes, including the MSCI USA Index, after the close on November 30. It is the first removal under MSCI’s new rule excluding non-operating companies. Analysts have estimated selling by index-tracking funds at about $2.8 billion. Bitcoin was little changed at around $73,800. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bernstein halves Nvidia target to $200, the 3rd broker in 2 days to step back over Huang
item.description:
Three brokers stepping back in two days removes an important source of support for Nvidia, just as the stock heads into results. Bernstein’s method matters for the wider AI trade. By cutting the multiple rather than earnings, it frames the problem as risk specific to Nvidia, not a slowdown in AI demand. That supports the rotation seen after hours, with AMD, Broadcom and Alphabet benefiting. For the indexes, Nvidia falling below a $4 trillion valuation would weigh heavily on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Futures and the Asian chip supply chain are likely to stay sensitive to any board announcement before November 17.

---

Bernstein still believes in Nvidia’s chips, just not in paying 25 times earnings while nobody knows who will be running the company.

Summary:

  • Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform from Outperform and cut his target to $200 from $400
  • He said leadership uncertainty, not weak chip sales, drove the move, and that Bernstein may not yet fully understand how deep the issue goes
  • Rasgon kept earnings forecasts unchanged, saying AI demand remains very strong, but halved the valuation multiple to about 12.7x fiscal 2028 earnings
  • Morgan Stanley stepped back on November 11, and Baird cut Nvidia to Neutral with a $200 target, down from $500
  • Nvidia fell roughly 8% after hours to around $160, on track to drop below a $4 trillion valuation

Bernstein has downgraded Nvidia to Market Perform from Outperform and halved its price target to $200 from $400. That makes it the third major brokerage in two days to step back from the stock as uncertainty over chief executive Jensen Huang’s future deepens.

Analyst Stacy Rasgon was clear that the move had nothing to do with weak chip sales. In a client note and a later CNBC appearance, he said the downgrade was driven by leadership uncertainty, after reports that Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Huang, who has acknowledged an extramarital affair. Rasgon wrote that Bernstein’s instinct is that it may not yet fully understand how deep the issue goes, and that it has chosen to step back to the sidelines for now. He also told CNBC that replacing Huang would be very difficult, and that it is not obvious who could succeed him.

The way Bernstein cut its target is the most telling part of the call. Rasgon kept his earnings forecasts unchanged, saying underlying AI demand remains very strong. Instead, he halved the valuation multiple he is willing to pay. The new $200 target equals roughly 12.7 times consensus earnings of about $15.75 a share for the fiscal year ending January 2028, down from about 25.4 times at the old $400 target. In Bernstein’s view, the business has not changed. What has changed is the price investors should pay for its future earnings, because of the risk around who will run it.

Bernstein is not alone. Morgan Stanley stepped back on November 11. Baird downgraded Nvidia to Neutral from Outperform and also cut its target to $200, from $500, citing uncertainty over Huang’s future as well as concerns about supply and visibility on 2027 spending.

Nvidia shares fell roughly 8% in after-hours trading to around $160, putting the company on track to slip below a $4 trillion market value. The drop pulled down AI infrastructure names such as CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer.

Even at $200, Bernstein’s target sits above where the shares are trading after hours, which suggests the bank sees the risk as uncertainty rather than collapse. The next markers are any board decision on Huang and Nvidia’s third-quarter results on November 17, when management will face questions on both demand and leadership.

item.title: CBA’s Chambers sees room for higher US 10-year yields despite the slide in oil prices
item.description:
A further rise in the 10-year yield toward and beyond 5% would keep the dollar supported. That matters most for USD/JPY, which is already near the 160 area where Japan has stepped up verbal warnings. Higher long-end yields would also weigh on gold, which has slipped below $4,000, and add pressure on richly valued tech stocks already hit by the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil is the key risk to the call. A sustained fall in crude would ease inflation fears and could cap yields, while a renewed rise linked to the Iran war would reinforce the move higher.

---

Cheaper oil might give Treasuries a breather, but CBA thinks growth and a hawkish Fed will keep pushing the 10-year yield higher.

Summary:

  • CBA’s Chambers says US Treasury yields have room to rise further
  • Yields jumped after a hot October CPI report and hawkish comments from Fed officials
  • Markets have largely priced in a December Fed hike
  • A sharp fall in oil prices may temporarily halt the rise in yields over the coming weeks
  • Chambers expects economic momentum and firmer Fed hike expectations to dominate, pushing the 10-year yield higher

US Treasury yields have further room to rise, even if the recent slide in oil prices slows their advance in the coming weeks, according to Commonwealth Bank of Australia rates strategist Chambers.

Yields have climbed sharply this week. A hotter than expected October inflation report, with consumer prices up 0.4% on the month and core prices up 0.3%, pushed the 10-year yield up 11 basis points to close to 5% on Tuesday. Hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials added to the move. Governor Christopher Waller raised the idea of a 50 basis point hike in December, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she favors at least two more quarter-point increases. Markets have largely priced in a December hike.

Chambers is watching two forces pulling in opposite directions. Oil prices have dropped sharply, which eases inflation concerns and could act as a temporary brake on yields. But he expects economic momentum and firmer expectations of Fed tightening to win out, pushing the 10-year yield higher in the near term.

That view fits a broader shift in bank forecasts this week. Deutsche Bank now expects quarter-point Fed hikes in December, January and March, while UBS sees hikes in December and March and has flagged the risk of a faster pace. If more forecasters move toward back-to-back hikes, longer-dated yields would have to adjust higher to reflect a higher expected path for policy.

Oil remains the main risk to the call. Crude has been volatile. Brent dipped below $90 a barrel earlier this week, then rebounded as attacks on shipping continued during the Iran war. A sustained fall in energy prices would weaken the inflation argument for further hikes, while a renewed spike would strengthen it.

For now, the balance looks tilted toward higher yields. That would keep the dollar supported and add pressure on assets that are sensitive to rates, from gold to richly valued technology stocks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ANZ says RBA hike bets have cooled, but 3.7% core inflation will keep it cautious
item.description:
Cooler RBA hike expectations take away one source of support for the Australian dollar, at a time when US yields are rising and the Fed is on a hiking path. That leaves the AUD exposed to further dollar strength. Sticky services inflation should limit how far Australian rate expectations can fall, though, which caps the downside for front-end bond yields. Lower oil prices help Australian headline inflation but do little for the domestic services pressures ANZ is focused on, so the RBA’s cautious stance looks likely to persist.

---

Growth is cooling, but services inflation isn’t, and that keeps the RBA from relaxing even as the case for another hike fades.

Summary:

  • ANZ economist Siddhant Kalra says expectations of further RBA rate hikes have cooled as Australia’s economy slows
  • Q3 trimmed mean inflation rose 1.0% q/q and 3.7% y/y, above forecasts and above the RBA’s 2% to 3% target band
  • Market services inflation posted its strongest annual gain since 2024
  • ANZ links market services prices to domestic capacity pressures
  • It says the strong result will keep the RBA cautious in the coming months

Expectations of further interest rate increases by the Reserve Bank of Australia have cooled as signs mount that the economy is slowing. But persistent inflation means the central bank is unlikely to drop its guard, according to ANZ economist Siddhant Kalra.

The pressure shows up most clearly in the RBA’s preferred core measure. The trimmed mean, which strips out the most extreme price moves each quarter, rose 1.0% in the third quarter and 3.7% from a year earlier. That was above forecasts and above the top of the central bank’s 2% to 3% target band. Market services inflation, which covers prices that depend mainly on local demand and labor costs, posted its strongest annual increase since 2024.

Kalra highlighted the services detail as the key point. Market services prices are closely linked to domestic capacity pressures, so they reflect how stretched the Australian economy is, rather than global influences such as oil prices or the currency. A strong reading suggests demand is still running up against the economy’s limits, which is the kind of inflation central banks find hardest to bring down.

ANZ said the strength of the result is likely to keep the RBA cautious in the coming months. That leaves the bank in an awkward position. Slowing growth argues against more tightening, while sticky underlying inflation argues against signaling that rates have peaked, let alone opening the door to cuts.

The global backdrop adds to the tension. Lower oil prices are easing pressure on headline inflation, but central banks elsewhere are leaning hawkish. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates in December after a hotter than expected October inflation report, and the Bank of Japan is also expected to hike.

For the RBA, the coming months are likely to be about patience rather than action. Unless services inflation eases, a meaningful shift toward lower rates looks some way off, even if the bar for another hike has risen. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank sees 3 straight Fed hikes after hot CPI, adding a January move
item.description:
A no-pause path into March is more hawkish than markets have priced beyond December. If other banks follow, it would likely be repriced through the front end of the Treasury curve and the dollar. That keeps USD/JPY pressed toward the 160 area where Tokyo is already warning, and it adds to the headwinds for gold. For equities, a faster sequence of hikes lands at an awkward moment, with AI stocks already under pressure from the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil remains the wildcard: renewed energy-driven inflation would strengthen the case for back-to-back hikes, while a sustained easing in crude would weaken it.

---

Deutsche Bank has turned UBS’s “faster tightening” risk into its base case, and the Fed debate is now about the pace after December, not whether December happens.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank now expects 25bp Fed hikes in December, January and March, adding a January move to its previous December and March path
  • That would lift the federal funds target range to 4.50% to 4.75%, from 3.75% to 4% now
  • The revision followed October CPI, which rose 0.4% m/m against a 0.3% forecast, and which the bank said showed broad-based gains
  • Deutsche Bank won’t rule out a 50bp December hike after Waller’s comments, but it isn’t the bank’s base case
  • UBS keeps a base case of hikes in December and March only
  • Markets price a December quarter-point hike at more than 95%, according to CME FedWatch

Deutsche Bank now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at each of its next three meetings, after adding a January increase to its forecast following a hotter than expected US inflation report. The bank sees quarter-point hikes in December, January and March. That would lift the federal funds target range to 4.50% to 4.75%, from 3.75% to 4% now.

Deutsche Bank had previously expected hikes in December and March, with a pause in January. The October consumer price report changed that view. Headline prices rose 0.4% on the month against forecasts of 0.3%, and the bank said the data continued to show broad-based gains.

The bank also addressed the idea of a larger move. Before the data, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50 basis point hike should be considered in December if price pressures accelerated, and Deutsche Bank said his comments opened that possibility. It would not rule out a half-point increase, but said a 50 basis point move is not its base case.

The revision puts Deutsche Bank at the more hawkish end of the major banks. UBS, for example, said this week it sees limited support on the rate-setting committee for a 50 basis point step. It keeps a base case of quarter-point hikes in December and March only, although it flagged the risk of more or faster tightening. The two views share a common thread: the debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how quickly it follows through.

Markets are close to fully pricing a December move. Traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting above 95%, according to CME FedWatch.

The path matters well beyond bonds. Three consecutive hikes would keep pressure on Treasury yields, which climbed close to 5% after the CPI release, and would support the dollar. It also raises the bar for assets that have struggled with higher rates, from gold, which has slipped back below $4,000 an ounce, to richly valued technology stocks. The next tests come from November’s labor market data and further Fed commentary before the December meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
